extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) involved in prosecution and interference matters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for establishing constructive and actual reduction to practice, the written-description/enablement requirements for constructive reduction, the tests and recognition/utility requirements for actual reduction, the doctrine of inurement, requirements for reasonable diligence (critical period, acceptable evidence, relation of work), and related pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 timing/effective filing date rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive reduction to practice via filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction to practice may be constructive when a patent application on the claimed invention is filed; the filing of a patent application serves as conception and constructive reduction to practice of the subject matter described in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventor need not provide evidence of conception or actual reduction to practice when relying on the content of the patent application. (Editor note: limited applicability to AIA/FITF applications; see MPEP §2159 et seq.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive reduction requires compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) / written description and enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on an earlier application as a constructive reduction to practice, the earlier application must meet 35 U.S.C. 120 and the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre‑AIA first paragraph) for the subject matter of the count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof requires sufficient disclosure under the 'how to use' and 'how to make' requirements; the written description must include all limitations of the interference count (or show any absent text is necessarily comprehended) and must be such that a person skilled in the art would give a construction that clearly supports each positive limitation. Examples/cases: Hyatt v. Boone; Kawai v. Metlesics; Bigham v. Godtfredsen (generic terms vs patentably distinct species).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual reduction to practice two‑prong test
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish actual reduction to practice in an interference, a party must (1) have constructed an embodiment or performed a process that met every element of the interference count, and (2) the embodiment or process must have operated for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eaton v. Evans articulates the two prongs. Actual reduction requires showing the invention in a physical/tangible form that shows every element of the count; the same evidence sufficient for constructive reduction may be insufficient for actual reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of testing for actual reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must have been sufficiently tested to demonstrate it will work for its intended purpose; testing required varies with complexity and nature of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work need not be at commercial stage. Simple devices may need only construction to show workability (King Instrument). Post‑reduction events can call reduction into question. Cases: Scott v. Finney; DSL Dynamic Sciences; Fitzgerald v. Arbib; Birmingham v. Randall (method‑of‑making inventions require satisfactory product testing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible nature of tests (relation to intended use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests conducted under laboratory or bench conditions can establish reduction to practice only if the conditions fully duplicate each and every condition of actual use or the evidence establishes a relationship between test conditions and the intended functional setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not required to duplicate every environmental condition, but the record must link test conditions to actual use (Gellert v. Wanberg; Wells v. Fremont).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition/appreciation requirement for reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A reduction to practice requires contemporaneous recognition and appreciation of the invention by the inventor; later recognition or testing generally cannot be used to show that contemporaneous appreciation existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of later testing may be admitted only to show an embodiment was produced and met the count's limitations. Inventor need not understand precisely why the invention works. Cases: Cooper v. Goldfarb; Meitzner v. Corte; Estee Lauder v. L'Oreal; Parker v. Frilette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inurement of another's recognition to the inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of the invention by a non‑inventor may inure to the benefit of the inventor only if three conditions are met: (1) the inventor conceived the invention, (2) the inventor expected the embodiment tested would work for the intended purpose, and (3) the inventor submitted the embodiment for testing for that intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the non‑inventor recognizes utility but the inventor did not submit the samples for testing of the intended purpose, the recognition does not inure. Example/case: Genentech, Inc. v. Chiron Corp.; Cooper v. Goldfarb (non‑communicated recognition does not inure).

rubrics_metrics.name: All limitations of a count must be reduced to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: In an interference, the physical embodiment reduced to practice must include every limitation of the count; every limitation is material and must be proved to establish an actual reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no reliance on the doctrine of equivalents in proving reduction to practice—remedy may be a preliminary motion to amend the count to conform to proofs. Cases: Fredkin v. Irasek; Meitzner v. Corte; Hull v. Bonis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known utility required at time of reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention is not actually reduced to practice unless its utility is known at the time of reduction (with exceptions such as plant and design inventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For compositions and methods, both composition and product must have practical utility. Demonstrated similarity to known compounds can establish utility for some inventions (Ciric v. Flanigen). Laboratory/animal tests may suffice where correlation to human utility exists or where tests prove utility for animals. Cases: Wiesner v. Weigert; Azar v. Burns; Engelhardt v. Judd; Rey‑Bellet v. Engelhardt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable utility insufficient to establish utility
rubrics_metrics.description: A probable utility, or a high degree of probability, does not by itself establish practical utility for reduction to practice; actual testing or a certainty‑foretellable utility is generally required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screening tests indicating possible utility are insufficient. However, evidence is judged as a whole and reasonable correlation between observed properties and suggested uses may suffice in some circumstances. Cases: Bindra v. Kelly; Wu v. Jucker; Nelson v. Bowler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence standard relates to both attorney and engineering diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Diligence under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) encompasses both 'attorney‑diligence' and 'engineering‑diligence' and does not require an inventor or attorney to drop all other work to concentrate solely on the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keizer v. Bradley; Emery v. Ronden. Reasonable diligence of an attorney (e.g., reasonable backlog handled chronologically) can inure to inventor's benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical period for establishing diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: For a first conceiver but later reducer, the critical period for diligence begins just prior to the entry into the field by the party who was first to reduce to practice and continues until the first conceiver reduces to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What constitutes entry into the field depends on what is being relied upon (conception plus reasonable diligence, actual reduction, constructive reduction by filing, or priority under 35 U.S.C. 119). Cases: Hull v. Davenport; Fritsch v. Lin; Rebstock v. Flouret; Justus v. Appenzeller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire diligence period must be accounted for by affirmative acts or acceptable excuses
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must account for the entire period during which diligence is required by showing reasonably continuous diligence through affirmative acts or acceptable excuses; mere statements are insufficient and short unexplained lapses can be fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonably continuous (not necessarily continuous) diligence is required (Perfect Surgical Techniques v. Olympus). Unexplained inactivity (even 2 days in some cases) can defeat diligence claims (In re Mulder; Fitzgerald v. Arbib; In re Mulder). Evidence must be specific with dates/facts. Some excuses (vacation, illness) may be considered; lack of funding or personnel often are not acceptable (Griffith v. Kanamaru; Litchfield v. Eigen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing diligence evidence as a whole (Perfect Surgical standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should weigh the entire body of evidence to determine reasonably continuous diligence; periods of inactivity do not automatically defeat diligence if the totality of evidence shows the invention was not abandoned or unreasonably delayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfect Surgical emphasizes holistic review; absence of daily records is not dispositive. In re Mulder is distinguished — lack of any evidence during the critical period is fatal, but short unexplained inactivity alone does not always destroy diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work relied upon must be directly related to the reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities used to show reasonable diligence must be directly related to reducing the specific subject matter of the count to practice; work on related inventions may sometimes be relied upon but only if it is sufficiently directed to attaining reduction of the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Naber v. Cricchi; Scott v. Koyama; In re Jolley; Ginos v. Nedelec (closely related inventions may be credited in some circumstances); Gunn v. Bosch (work on different inventions that merely fortuitously produce the actual reduction is not diligence). Preparation of foreign filings and related activities can count (Broos v. Barton; De Solms v. Schoenwald).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence in preparing and filing patent application
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable diligence in the preparation and filing of the patent application (including attorney work) inures to the benefit of the inventor; conception may be established when a draft application is finished by the attorney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney need only exercise reasonable diligence (e.g., six days to execute and file is acceptable). Reasonable backlog and work on related cases that contributed can be credited. Absence of daily discussions or revisions does not alone show abandonment. Cases: Haskell v. Coleburne; Bey v. Kollonitsch; Perfect Surgical.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of diligence period marked by actual or constructive reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of the critical diligence period is fixed by either an actual reduction to practice or a constructive reduction to practice (filing of an application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justus v. Appenzeller: it does not matter whether the end is actual or constructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑AIA regime applicability (timing rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any application filed before March 16, 2013 is governed by pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103; certain applications filed on or after March 16, 2013 that claim benefit to an earlier filing date may also be governed by pre‑AIA 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for continued examination or national stage entry do not constitute filing of a new application; see MPEP §§2159 and 2150 et seq. for applicability determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective filing date rules under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102
rubrics_metrics.description: The effective filing date is normally the actual U.S. filing date unless: (A) the application is a continuation/divisional with 35 U.S.C. 120 satisfied (earliest date in chain), (B) a continuation‑in‑part—claims not supported by parent have the new filing date while fully supported claims have the parent's date, or (C) proper claim to 35 U.S.C. 119(e) provisional (claims fully supported by provisional have provisional filing date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The effective filing date for an application that entered the national stage under 35 U.S.C. 371 is the international filing date; the foreign priority document filing date itself is not the effective filing date for pre‑AIA 102 claims (though it may overcome certain references). See MPEP §§1893.03, 211.01(c), 1895.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) first when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should first consider whether a reference qualifies as prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) because that section results in a statutory bar to obtaining a patent (i.e., publication/issue date more than one year prior to the effective filing date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the last day of the one‑year grace period falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday, filing on the next business day avoids the statutory bar (Ex parte Olah). Changes to 37 CFR 1.6(a)(2) and 1.10 regarding Priority Mail Express do not affect applicant's concurrent right to defer to the next business day when the last day falls on a weekend/holiday.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use or sale more than one year before filing -> 102(b) statutory bar
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is evidence of public use or sale activity more than one year prior to the effective filing date, the proper rejection is under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b), which is a statutory bar, rather than under 102(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere public knowledge of the invention does not by itself warrant a 102(b) rejection; public knowledge may support 102(a) instead. See MPEP §§2132 and 2133.03(a).
